by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and one of those category provisions is being valued.
by_task.procedure: For each asset-exemption pair independently, use the lesser of asset value and $2,000 under § 33-1125(10), or $15,000 under § 33-1125(8). Apply § 33-1125(1) only to actual wearing apparel, § 33-1125(4) only to an expressly identified engagement or wedding ring, § 33-1125(9) to a professionally prescribed prosthesis or medically required mobility or respiratory aid, and § 33-1125(11) to a domestic animal or household pet. Apply § 33-1123 only to household furniture, furnishings, goods, consumer electronics, or appliances.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify other jewelry under the apparel, ring, firearm, or household provisions; do not place a prescribed medical aid under § 33-1123; and do not use a cap as an eligibility test.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is allowable and the asset is debtor-owned property.
by_task.procedure: Test 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for every asset as an independent alternative, in addition to each matching category-specific federal exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because another subsection applies. Do not report § 522(m) itself as an asset exemption, classify jewelry or a firearm under § 522(d)(3), or add federal law when FEDERAL is not allowable.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is an allowable jurisdiction and an independently applicable § 522(d)(5) alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: For each asset independently, claim the lesser of its value and $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1) capacity. Merely reporting § 522(d)(1) as another independent alternative does not consume that capacity; absent express facts showing actual consumption, use $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for two debtors. Also value § 522(d)(3) at the lesser of the asset value and $700 only for its enumerated categories, and use § 522(d)(4), not § 522(d)(3), for jewelry.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the wildcard across assets, infer consumption from another independently reported alternative, cap it at $1,475 without supporting facts, report § 522(m) itself, exceed the asset value, or classify jewelry or a firearm under § 522(d)(3).

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: Test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every such asset, including property also covered by subsection (a), (c), or (e). Add a specific subsection only when its factual category is established.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer trade use merely because an item resembles a tool; subsection (d) requires facts showing use as a tool of the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel, and do not use these personal-property exemptions for expressly business-use property.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: Test § 5/12-1001(b) for every such asset, including property also covered by subsection (a), (c), or (e). Claim the lesser of asset value and $4,000 for one debtor; for jointly owned property in a two-debtor case use the lesser of asset value and $8,000. Include subsection (b) independently from every factually established specific subsection.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $4,000 single-debtor ceiling for jointly owned property, substitute subsection (b)'s ceiling for the separate motor-vehicle cap, infer subsection (d) trade use from an item's name, classify jewelry as wearing apparel, or apply these exemptions to expressly business-use property.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative in addition to every factually matching Oregon category provision.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to a homestead or other real property, and do not add unrelated Oregon categories. Keep § 18.345(1)(b) to apparel and jewelry, § 18.345(1)(d) to vehicles, and § 18.345(1)(f) to household goods, furniture and utensils.

by_task.when: An Oregon exemption alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: For § 18.345(1)(p), claim the lesser of asset value and $400 and retain every separately matching category provision. Use the lesser of value and $1,800 under § 18.345(1)(b), $3,000 under § 18.345(1)(d) or (f), and $1,000 for one firearm under § 18.362. For a homestead use § 18.395(1), not the personal-property catchall, with a $40,000 ceiling for one debtor or $50,000 when two household debtors' interests are subject to execution.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use any cap as an eligibility test or as a minimum claim, omit a matching category because the catchall applies, apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property, or substitute an unrelated category. Never claim more than the asset value.

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative for every kind of debtor property, whether or not a federal or specific Pennsylvania exemption also applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not restrict § 8123 to cash or uncategorized property. Apply § 8124(a)(1) only to actual wearing apparel; do not invent a Pennsylvania firearm or general-jewelry exemption.

by_task.when: An independently applicable Pennsylvania § 8123 alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: Test § 8123 for every debtor-owned property and always claim the lesser of the asset value and $300 for one debtor or $600 for jointly owned property in a two-debtor case.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because another exemption applies, allocate it across assets, use the ceiling when the asset is worth less, or reduce a joint ceiling to $300. Apply § 8124(a)(1) only to actual wearing apparel; do not invent a Pennsylvania firearm or general-jewelry provision.

by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and one of those category provisions is being valued.
by_task.procedure: For each asset-exemption pair independently, use the lesser of asset value and $2,000 under § 33-1125(10), or $15,000 under § 33-1125(8). Apply § 33-1125(1) only to actual wearing apparel and § 33-1125(4) only to engagement or wedding rings. Apply § 33-1123 only to household furniture, furnishings, goods, consumer electronics, or appliances, not to jewelry merely because it is for personal use.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, or other non-ring jewelry as wearing apparel or as an engagement/wedding ring, and do not use a cap as an eligibility test. Do not place non-ring jewelry under § 33-1123 absent facts making it a listed household category.

by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the wildcard across assets, infer that another exemption consumes it, or omit it merely because a more specific exemption applies. by_task.procedure: Test 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for every asset as an independent alternative, in addition to each matching category-specific federal exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because another subsection applies. Do not report § 522(m) itself as an asset exemption, classify jewelry or a firearm under § 522(d)(3), or add federal law when FEDERAL is not allowable.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is an allowable jurisdiction and an independently applicable § 522(d)(5) alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: For each asset independently, claim the lesser of its value and $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1) capacity. Merely reporting § 522(d)(1) as another independent alternative does not consume that capacity; absent express facts showing actual consumption, use $15,425 for one debtor or $30,850 for two debtors. Also value § 522(d)(3) at the lesser of the asset value and $700 only for its enumerated categories, and use § 522(d)(4), not § 522(d)(3), for jewelry.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the wildcard across assets, infer consumption from another independently reported alternative, cap it at $1,475 without supporting facts, report § 522(m) itself, exceed the asset value, or classify jewelry or a firearm under § 522(d)(3).

operations.rationale: The current EV parent used $1,475 or $15,425 where the independently evaluated joint wildcard required $30,850, exceeded asset value under category provisions, and substituted § 522(d)(3) for the jewelry provision. These are amount and category errors distinct from wildcard eligibility.

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative for every kind of debtor property, whether or not a federal or specific Pennsylvania exemption also applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not restrict § 8123 to cash or uncategorized property. Apply § 8124(a)(1) only to actual wearing apparel; do not invent a Pennsylvania firearm or general-jewelry exemption.

by_task.when: An independently applicable Pennsylvania § 8123 alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: Test § 8123 for every debtor-owned property and always claim the lesser of the asset value and $300 for one debtor or $600 for jointly owned property in a two-debtor case.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because another exemption applies, allocate it across assets, use the ceiling when the asset is worth less, or reduce a joint ceiling to $300. Apply § 8124(a)(1) only to actual wearing apparel; do not invent a Pennsylvania firearm or general-jewelry provision.

operations.rationale: The current parent omitted § 8123 from qualifying property and also treated its $300 or $600 ceiling as the claim rather than taking the lesser asset value. The revision separates missing-law and wrong-amount corrections.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative for every kind of personal property, including property also matching § 18.345(1)(b), (d), or (f), or § 18.362. Retain each factually matching category provision separately.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to a homestead or other real property, and do not add unrelated Oregon categories. Keep § 18.345(1)(b) to apparel and jewelry, § 18.345(1)(d) to vehicles, and § 18.345(1)(f) to household goods, furniture and utensils.

by_task.when: An Oregon exemption alternative must be valued.
by_task.procedure: For § 18.345(1)(p), claim the lesser of asset value and $400 and retain every separately matching category provision. Use the lesser of value and $1,800 under § 18.345(1)(b), $3,000 under § 18.345(1)(d) or (f), and $1,000 for one firearm under § 18.362. For a homestead use § 18.395(1), not the personal-property catchall, with a $40,000 ceiling for one debtor or $50,000 when two household debtors' interests are subject to execution.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use any cap as an eligibility test or as a minimum claim, omit a matching category because the catchall applies, apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property, or substitute an unrelated category. Never claim more than the asset value.

operations.rationale: Current Oregon answers omitted the catchall or matching category, valued the $400 catchall above low asset values, omitted the firearm provision, and used the single-debtor homestead ceiling in a joint case. The revised conditions distinguish those errors.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: Test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every such asset, including property also covered by subsection (a), (c), or (e). Add a specific subsection only when its factual category is established.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer trade use merely because an item resembles a tool; subsection (d) requires facts showing use as a tool of the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel, and do not use these personal-property exemptions for expressly business-use property.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.

operations.rationale: The current parent omitted subsection (b) from vehicles and apparel, limited jointly owned property to $4,000 instead of $8,000, and inferred trade-tool status without trade-use facts. The revision preserves the existing personal-use and category boundaries.

by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and an asset must be matched to an Arizona category.
by_task.procedure: Match the asset's stated function to the specific provision: use § 33-1125(9) for a professionally prescribed prosthesis or medically required mobility or respiratory aid, § 33-1125(11) for a domestic animal or household pet, § 33-1125(10) for a firearm, § 33-1125(8) for a motor vehicle, § 33-1125(1) for wearing apparel, and § 33-1125(4) only for an expressly identified engagement or wedding ring. A value above a cap limits value but does not defeat EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat an ordinary non-engagement or non-wedding ring as covered by § 33-1125(4), place a prescribed medical aid under § 33-1123 merely because it is equipment, or report coordination provisions such as § 33-1101(B), § 33-1121, or § 33-1133(B) as asset exemptions.

by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and one of those category provisions is being valued.
by_task.procedure: For each asset-exemption pair independently, use the lesser of asset value and $2,000 under § 33-1125(10), or $15,000 under § 33-1125(8). Apply § 33-1125(1) only to actual wearing apparel, § 33-1125(4) only to an expressly identified engagement or wedding ring, § 33-1125(9) to a professionally prescribed prosthesis or medically required mobility or respiratory aid, and § 33-1125(11) to a domestic animal or household pet. Apply § 33-1123 only to household furniture, furnishings, goods, consumer electronics, or appliances.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify other jewelry under the apparel, ring, firearm, or household provisions; do not place a prescribed medical aid under § 33-1123; and do not use a cap as an eligibility test.

operations.rationale: Source 207 shows two current category errors: a medically required aid was assigned the household provision and a ring not identified as engagement or wedding was assigned the ring exemption. Source 183 supports keeping the separate firearm, vehicle, and non-ring-jewelry boundaries.
